title: Discover the Lost Horror Series Deemed Too Shocking for BBC Television (1967)
description:
in History, Television |   	October 6th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

High cul­ture and new tech­nol­o­gy have nev­er been a nat­ur­al pair­ing.
body:
in History, Television |   	October 6th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

High cul­ture and new tech­nol­o­gy have nev­er been a nat­ur­al pair­ing. As our dig­i­tal era has often under­scored, media inno­va­tions tend to be adopt­ed ear­li­est to deliv­er the most puerile, sen­sa­tion-dri­ven con­tent, with the more respectable stuff ben­e­fit­ing only lat­er. When the BBC was intro­duc­ing col­or broad­cast­ing in the mid-nine­teen-six­ties, for instance, it was used for the likes of Thun­der­birds, The Avengers, and The Ben­ny Hill Show, respectable though those pro­grams may now seem com­pared to what main­stream tele­vi­sion would become in lat­er decades. No col­or pro­duc­tion of that peri­od aimed quite as low as the anthol­o­gy series Late Night Hor­ror — or has since been raised so high in the minds of those who remem­ber it.
“We must do every­thing we can from the very begin­ning to stim­u­late sus­pense, ten­sion, atmos­phere, poten­tial hor­ror and HORROR!” the show’s pro­duc­er Har­ry Moore wrote in a memo to his staff in 1967. “If there is blood, let’s see the blood.” Just a few years before choco­late syrup cir­cled the drain in Alfred Hitch­cock­’s Psy­cho, whose faint­ly anachro­nis­tic black-and-white cin­e­matog­ra­phy only inten­si­fied its scari­ness, Late Night Hor­ror had a man­date to paint the small screen red. As cul­tur­al leg­end has it, only six episodes were broad­cast before com­plaints about its pow­er to shock and dis­turb, or per­haps con­cerns about its increas­ing extrem­i­ty, got it the axe from BBC man­age­ment.
The idea that Late Night Hor­ror was sim­ply too scary for tele­vi­sion — or British pub­lic tele­vi­sion of the late six­ties, in any case — has become more com­pelling over the decades in part because so lit­tle of the series itself has sur­vived to receive the judg­ment of lat­er gen­er­a­tions of view­ers. Only in 2016 did archivists dis­cov­er a film copy of “The Corpse Can’t Play,” a sto­ry set at a chil­dren’s par­ty that takes a dead­ly turn. Writ­ten by the pro­lif­ic Eng­lish nov­el­ist John Burke, the episode’s slow burn leads up to a grotesque fin­ish that con­trasts almost cheek­i­ly with the mun­dane domes­tic­i­ty of its set­ting. Alas, the recov­ered print was in black-and-white, so we don’t get to see the col­ors, san­guineous and oth­er­wise, that would have made such an impact on view­ers of near­ly six decades ago.
Just this year, anoth­er episode was redis­cov­ered: “No Such Thing as a Vam­pire” by Richard Math­e­son, author of I Am Leg­end and no few­er than six­teen Twi­light Zone episodes. As of now, the oth­er four episodes remain miss­ing, and pre­sum­ably erased under the per­pet­u­al­ly cash-strapped BBC’s pol­i­cy of eras­ing tapes for re-use in the mid-twen­ti­eth cen­tu­ry. One of them, “William and Mary,” was based on a Roald Dahl sto­ry that had been pre­vi­ous­ly adapt­ed in 1961 for the series Way Out, and would be adapt­ed again in 1979 for Tales of the Unex­pect­ed. At this point, even if a com­plete set of Late Night Hor­ror tapes were to turn up in some­one’s shed, the real­i­ty of the show could hard­ly be expect­ed to com­pete with what its scat­tered frag­ments — espe­cial­ly its still-chill­ing open­ing sequence — inspire us to imag­ine. As every seri­ous hor­ror fan knows, it’s what we don’t see that scares us most.
via Men­tal Floss

title: In 1704, Isaac Newton Predicted That the World Will End in 2060
description: We have become quite used to pro­nounce­ments of doom, from sci­en­tists pre­dict­ing the sixth mass extinc­tion due to the mea­sur­able effects
body:
We have become quite used to pro­nounce­ments of doom, from sci­en­tists pre­dict­ing the sixth mass extinc­tion due to the mea­sur­able effects of cli­mate change, and from reli­gion­ists declar­ing the apoc­a­lypse due to a sur­feit of sin. It’s almost impos­si­ble to imag­ine these two groups of peo­ple agree­ing on any­thing oth­er than the omi­nous por­tent of their respec­tive mes­sages. But in the ear­ly days of the sci­en­tif­ic revolution—the days of Shake­speare’s con­tem­po­rary Fran­cis Bacon, and lat­er 17th cen­tu­ry Descartes—it was not at all unusu­al to find both kinds of rea­son­ing, or unrea­son­ing, in the same per­son, along with beliefs in mag­ic, div­ina­tion, astrol­o­gy, etc.
Yet even in this mael­strom of het­ero­dox thought and prac­tices, Sir Isaac New­ton stood out as a par­tic­u­lar­ly odd co-exis­tence of eso­teric bib­li­cal prophe­cy, occult beliefs, and a rigid, for­mal math­e­mat­ics that not only adhered to the induc­tive sci­en­tif­ic method, but also expand­ed its poten­tial by apply­ing gen­er­al axioms to spe­cif­ic cas­es.
Yet many of Newton’s gen­er­al prin­ci­ples would seem total­ly inim­i­cal to the nat­u­ral­ism of most physi­cists today. As he was for­mu­lat­ing the prin­ci­ples of grav­i­ty and three laws of motion, for exam­ple, New­ton also sought the leg­endary Philosopher’s Stone and attempt­ed to turn met­al to gold. More­over, the devout­ly reli­gious New­ton wrote the­o­log­i­cal trea­tis­es inter­pret­ing Bib­li­cal prophe­cies and pre­dict­ing the end of the world. The date he arrived at? 2060.

New­ton seems, writes sci­ence blog Anoth­er Pale Blue Dot, “as con­fi­dent of his pre­dic­tions in this realm as he was in the ratio­nal world of sci­ence.” In a 1704 let­ter exhib­it­ed at Jerusalem’s Hebrew Uni­ver­si­ty, above, New­ton describes his “rec­coning”:
So then the time times & half a time are 42 months or 1260 days or three years & an half, rec­coning twelve months to a yeare & 30 days to a month as was done in the Cal­en­dar of the prim­i­tive year. And the days of short lived Beasts being put for the years of lived [sic] king­doms, the peri­od of 1260 days, if dat­ed from the com­plete con­quest of the three kings A.C. 800, will end A.C. 2060. It may end lat­er, but I see no rea­son for its end­ing soon­er.
New­ton fur­ther demon­strates his con­fi­dence in the next sen­tence, writ­ing that his intent, “though not to assert” an answer, should in any event “put a stop the rash con­jec­tures of fan­ci­full men who are fre­quent­ly pre­dict­ing the time of the end.” Indeed. So how did he arrive at this num­ber? New­ton applied a rig­or­ous method, that is to be sure.
If you have the patience for an exhaus­tive descrip­tion of how he worked out his pre­dic­tion using the Book of Daniel, you may read one here by his­to­ri­an of sci­ence Stephen Sno­be­len, who also points out how wide­spread the inter­est in Newton’s odd beliefs has become, reach­ing across every con­ti­nent, though schol­ars have known about this side of the Enlight­en­ment giant for a long time.
For a sense of the exact­ing, yet com­plete­ly bizarre fla­vor of Newton’s prophet­ic cal­cu­la­tions, see anoth­er New­ton let­ter at the top of the post, tran­scribed below.
Prop. 1. The 2300 prophet­ick days did not com­mence before the rise of the lit­tle horn of the He Goat.
2 Those day [sic] did not com­mence a[f]ter the destruc­tion of Jerusalem & ye Tem­ple by the Romans A.[D.] 70.
3 The time times & half a time did not com­mence before the year 800 in wch the Popes suprema­cy com­menced
4 They did not com­mence after the re[ig]ne of Gre­go­ry the 7th. 1084
5 The 1290 days did not com­mence b[e]fore the year 842.
6 They did not com­mence after the reigne of Pope Greg. 7th. 1084
7 The dif­f­ence [sic] between the 1290 & 1335 days are a parts of the sev­en weeks.
There­fore the 2300 years do not end before ye year 2132 nor after 2370.
The time times & half time do n[o]t end before 2060 nor after [2344]
The 1290 days do not begin [this should read: end] before 2090 [New­ton might mean: 2132] nor after 1374 [sic; New­ton prob­a­bly means 2374]
The edi­to­r­i­al inser­tions are Pro­fes­sor Snobelen’s, who thinks the let­ter dates “from after 1705,” and that “the shaky hand­writ­ing sug­gests a date of com­po­si­tion late in Newton’s life.” What­ev­er the exact date, we see him much less cer­tain here; New­ton push­es around some oth­er dates—2344, 2090 (or 2132), 2374. All of them seem arbi­trary, but “giv­en the nice round­ness of the num­ber,” writes Moth­er­board, “and the fact that it appears in more than one let­ter,” 2060 has become his most mem­o­rable dat­ing for the apoc­a­lypse.
It’s impor­tant to note that New­ton didn’t believe the world would “end” in the sense of cease to exist or burn up in holy flames. His end times phi­los­o­phy resem­bles that of a sur­pris­ing num­ber of cur­rent day evan­gel­i­cals: Christ would return and reign for a mil­len­ni­um, the Jew­ish dias­po­ra would return to Israel and would, he wrote, set up “a flour­ish­ing and ever­last­ing King­dom.” We hear such state­ments often from tel­e­van­ge­lists, school boards, gov­er­nors, and pres­i­den­tial can­di­dates.
As many peo­ple have argued, despite Newton’s con­cep­tion of his sci­en­tif­ic work as a bul­wark against oth­er the­olo­gies, it ulti­mate­ly became a foun­da­tion for Deism and Nat­u­ral­ism, and has allowed sci­en­tists to make accu­rate pre­dic­tions for hun­dreds of years. 20th cen­tu­ry physics may have shown us a much more rad­i­cal­ly unsta­ble uni­verse than New­ton ever imag­ined, but his the­o­ries are, as Isaac Asi­mov would put it, “not so much wrong as incom­plete,” and still essen­tial to our under­stand­ing of cer­tain fun­da­men­tal phe­nom­e­na. But as fas­ci­nat­ing and curi­ous as Newton’s oth­er inter­ests may be, there’s no more rea­son to cred­it his prophet­ic cal­cu­la­tions than those of the Mil­lerites, Harold Camp­ing, or any oth­er apoc­a­lyp­tic dooms­day sect.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2015.

title: Artists Frida Kahlo & Diego Rivera Visit Leon Trotsky in Mexico: Vintage Footage from 1938
description:
in Art |   	October 5th, 2026  1 Comment
	
			

	

Here’s some rare footage of the great Mex­i­can painters Diego Rivera and Fri­da Kahlo pay­ing a
body:
in Art |   	October 5th, 2026  1 Comment
	
			

	

Here’s some rare footage of the great Mex­i­can painters Diego Rivera and Fri­da Kahlo pay­ing a vis­it to exiled Sovi­et rev­o­lu­tion­ary Leon Trot­sky and his wife, Natalia Sedo­va, in Coyoacán, Mex­i­co, in 1938.
The Trot­skys had arrived the year before, after Rivera peti­tioned the gov­ern­ment of Pres­i­dent Lázaro Cár­de­nas to grant the con­tro­ver­sial Marx­ist leader and the­o­rist sanc­tu­ary in Mex­i­co. When the Trot­skys arrived on a Nor­we­gian oil tanker at the port city of Tampi­co in Jan­u­ary of 1937, Rivera was not well, but Kahlo board­ed the ship to wel­come the Trot­skys and accom­pa­nied them on an armored train to Mex­i­co City. She invit­ed the Trot­skys to stay at her fam­i­ly home, La Casa Azul (the Blue House) in Coyoacán, now a sec­tion of Mex­i­co City. By the time this footage was tak­en by a vis­it­ing Amer­i­can named Ivan Heisler, Trot­sky and Kahlo had either had, or were about to have, a brief affair, and the friend­ship between the two cou­ples would soon fall apart. In ear­ly 1939 Trot­sky moved to anoth­er house in the same neigh­bor­hood, where he was assas­si­nat­ed in August of 1940.

It’s hard to rely 100% on ads, and your con­tri­bu­tions will help us con­tin­ue pro­vid­ing the best free cul­tur­al and edu­ca­tion­al mate­ri­als to learn­ers every­where. title: 300 Years Before ChatGPT, Jonathan Swift’s Gulliver’s Travels Imagined Machines Writing Books and Producing Knowledge (1726)
description: The print­ing press was invent­ed in the mid­dle of the fif­teenth cen­tu­ry, and it’s been down­hill for the writ­ten word ever since. Even befo
body:
The print­ing press was invent­ed in the mid­dle of the fif­teenth cen­tu­ry, and it’s been down­hill for the writ­ten word ever since. Even before then, argu­ments that the vol­ume of writ­ing being done far out­stripped the val­ue of that writ­ing sure­ly weren’t unheard of. What­ev­er the era, the most inci­sive remarks on the appar­ent vic­to­ry of ver­bal quan­ti­ty over ver­bal qual­i­ty tend to have come from writ­ers them­selves. No less a satirist than Jonathan Swift made it one of his many tar­gets in Gul­liv­er’s Trav­els (1726), imag­in­ing an elab­o­rate machine of wood and wire called “the Engine” (see illus­tra­tion above) that auto­mat­i­cal­ly gen­er­ates text, though few remem­ber it — or rather, few remem­bered it until the rise of large lan­guage mod­els in the real world.
Gul­liv­er encoun­ters that tech­no­log­i­cal mar­vel, the Engine, at an insti­tu­tion called the Acad­e­my of Pro­jec­tors in the city of Laga­do. Swift’s pro­tag­o­nist records its cre­ator’s expla­na­tion as fol­lows: “Every one knew how labo­ri­ous the usu­al method is of attain­ing to arts and sci­ences; where­as, by his con­trivance, the most igno­rant per­son, at a rea­son­able charge, and with a lit­tle bod­i­ly labor, might write books in phi­los­o­phy, poet­ry, pol­i­tics, laws, math­e­mat­ics, and the­ol­o­gy, with­out the least assis­tance from genius or study.” The Engine’s oper­a­tion, with its unwieldy, clack­ing com­po­nents and a scram­bling staff of young crankers, read­ers, and scribes, may strike us as bizarre, just as it did audi­ences in the eigh­teenth cen­tu­ry. But in our time, when stu­dents can write their papers lit­er­al­ly with­out giv­ing it a thought (to say noth­ing of what their pro­fes­sors may be get­ting up to), its con­cept now sounds all too plau­si­ble.
“This is one of the ear­li­est known men­tions of a machine that could be con­sid­ered as a com­put­er in lit­er­a­ture, more than a hun­dred years pri­or to the first cal­cu­lat­ing engine designs by Charles Bab­bage,” writes Chris Gar­cia at the web site of the Com­put­er His­to­ry Muse­um. “The Engine might be seen as a com­put­er, but per­haps it’s bet­ter thought of as a sort of ran­dom-num­ber gen­er­a­tor,” spout­ing out whichev­er words of the local lan­guage that cor­re­spond with the dig­its. That post dates from ten years, near­ly to the day, before the launch of Chat­G­PT, which changed the gen­er­al pub­lic’s ideas about what com­put­ers can and can’t do. We may dis­agree about whether a machine can tru­ly gen­er­ate “a com­plete body of all arts and sci­ences,” as the Engine’s inven­tor intends, but it no longer sounds like sheer­est fan­ta­sy.
Swift had in mind not engi­neers of arti­fi­cial intel­li­gence but the Roy­al Soci­ety, whose enthu­si­asm for sci­en­tif­ic knowl­edge and exper­i­men­ta­tion he saw as insuf­fi­cient­ly teth­ered to real­i­ty, or at least prac­ti­cal­i­ty. In addi­tion to the Engine, writes lit­er­a­ture pro­fes­sor Robin Bates, “Swift imag­ines sci­en­tists attempt­ing to extract sun­beams from cucum­bers, soft­en mar­ble into pil­lows and pin­cush­ions, replace silk­worms with spi­ders (and hav­ing them eat bright­ly col­ored flies so the threads will be pre-dyed), mix paint by smell, reassem­ble orig­i­nal food stuffs from excre­ment, and build hous­es from the top down (in imi­ta­tion of the bee and the spi­der).” His satire holds up today thanks to his under­stand­ing that, “for all the promis­es of the Enlight­en­ment, the Age of Rea­son, and the Sci­en­tif­ic and Tech­no­log­i­cal Rev­o­lu­tions,” our attempts to change the world “founder the moment we start ignor­ing human nature.” But who needs human nature, the Pro­jec­tors of today might argue, when you’ve got enough com­pute?

title: Through Fictional Self-Portraits, Tang Shuo Visualizes an Ancestral Archive
description: As a child in Dashishan Village in southern China, Tang Shuo was afraid of snakes. He and several generations of the Tang family lived together in
body:
As a child in Dashishan Village in southern China, Tang Shuo was afraid of snakes. He and several generations of the Tang family lived together in a small community and farmed the land, tending to crops and sheep and encountering the occasional reptile. In a vivid new painting on linen, the artist confronts this adolescent fear as he envisions himself grasping a sleek, black serpent, its recently shed skin lying beneath them.
Long interested in his ancestry and familial connection to the land, Tang once again journeys to his home territory for Borrowed History, his first solo exhibition in New York. This body of work extends the artist’s approach to questioning how our heritage informs our understanding of who we are and how we got here. Working from photographs of himself, Tang renders his likeness in a variety of positions he envisions his kin having occupied. There’s “The Migrant” carrying a small sack slung over his back, for example, and “The Settler” hoisting a tree trunk with tools and bones scattered in the background. 
“The Migrant” (2026), oil on linen, 100 x 80 centimeters
Tinged with magical realism—Tang cites Gabriel García Márquez’s One Hundred Years of Solitude as an influence—the paintings reach backward to imagine the lives of the artist’s ancestors. Lush forests and candy-colored clouds envelop the scenes as a way to connect eras and generations. Nature and the terrain occupied, the artist suggests, is the throughline that tethers him to those who came before.
Although the specific scenes are fictional, Tang also considers his practice to be one of archiving “a world that is disappearing,” a statement says. “When he was a child, more than two hundred people lived in Dashishan; today, only a dozen or so remain. He continues to document the inhabitants and stories of the village and will eventually publish a book recording its history, which he describes as his ‘own bible.'”
Borrowed History is on view from October 8 to November 7 at Plato Gallery. Explore more of Tang’s works on Instagram.

title: Pre-Columbian Archaeology Meets Science Fiction in Max Lehman's Quirky Sculptures
description: In archaeology, discoveries typically prompt more questions than answers. For Max Lehman, who studies Pre-Columbian art history, what we don’t kno
body:
In archaeology, discoveries typically prompt more questions than answers. For Max Lehman, who studies Pre-Columbian art history, what we don’t know—and may never—about ancient peoples and civilizations is what makes the discipline so compelling. The ancient Mayans, for example, bedecked their elaborate temples with images on carved rock slabs, and the Aztec sun stone, or calendar stone, is a remarkable example of Mexica sculpture.
Lehman’s work has one foot in the advanced civilizations of the past and another in the distant future, a time long after today’s developments around robotic and machine learning technologies. His current show Ancestral Androids at Hecho a Mano delves into a kind of future past inspired by science fiction, where modern tech and prehistoric visual culture merge in unexpected and idiosyncratic ways.
“Petro who is Predicting the Unpredictable” (2026), ceramic with acrylic and metallic paint, 12 x 11 x 8 inches
The New Mexico-based artist imagines his pieces being excavated by archaeologists many years down the line, when their exact origin and function have been lost to time. “I resist providing complete explanations because archaeology rarely offers certainty,” Lehman says in a statement. “We reconstruct civilizations from fragments, projecting ourselves into the spaces left empty by time.”
Lehman’s work also nudges the nature of information itself, as we find ourselves in an era of data and archives (digital and otherwise) at a scale unprecedented in human history. It begs the question: in the next thousand years or more, what information will remain? And how will AI influence which stories are told and what is considered fact or myth? These technologies are already reshaping our minds.
“Artists understandably worry about AI appropriating their ideas,” Lehman says. “My own work, however, remains deeply rooted in the physical act of making—there is still no machine that can throw a ceramic vessel with the intuition, hesitation, and accumulated experience of human hands. Clay continues to preserve evidence of the maker in ways that cannot be simulated.”
“The Malachite Mage” (2026), ceramic with acrylic and metallic paint, 14 x 14 x 7 inches
Vividly colorful characters with titles like “The Mother of Machines” and “Sapphire Sage” nod to sacred figures with enigmatic associations. They’re cartoonish, and occasionally clownish, with expressions that read as slightly unsettling. It’s almost as if the characters are devoid of any real feeling, like both a robot or a carved stone. Additional faces often appear on bellies or foreheads, suggesting collectivity and shared consciousness. “The sculptures ask us to consider what happens when artificial beings become old enough to have ancestors, old enough to leave ruins, and old enough for their own history to become myth,” the artist says.
Ancestral Androids continues through November 1 in Santa Fe. See more on Lehman’s Instagram.

title: Monumental Sculptures by Sharif Bey Meditate on Identity and Objecthood in 'Homecoming'
description: From nail-cloaked ceramic vessels to larger-than-life busts influenced by African and Oceanic visual culture, Sharif Bey’s bold works summon the c
body:
From nail-cloaked ceramic vessels to larger-than-life busts influenced by African and Oceanic visual culture, Sharif Bey’s bold works summon the complexities of heritage, identity, and society. In his ceramic and mixed-media Guardian Series and Crown Series, calm yet imposing figures evoke the Benin Bronzes, ceremonial masking traditions, the giant Moai stone heads of Easter Island, and more.
Bey has long been interested in the commanding nature of objects, especially the ways in which colonialist forces have mined cultural heritage. The Benin Bronzes, which artisans created during the 14th century in what is now Nigeria, are a prime example: British troops looted thousands of plaques in 1897, and The British Museum, The Met, the Smithsonian, Chicago’s Field Museum, and more keep them in their collections. Some have been repatriated, but most remain in Western institutional collections.
‘Crown Series’ installation view, (left to right) “Crown Series: Iris” (2024), “Crown Series: Sadie” (2024), “Crown Series: Opal” (2024). Photo by Kohler Co., courtesy of the John Michael Kohler Arts Center
In Sharif Bey: Homecoming at The Andy Warhol Museum, the title of which nods to the artist’s background growing up in Pittsburgh, works like “Crown Series: Iris” and “Guardian Series: Blink” possess a deified air. Ceramic beads complement rusty nails, spikes, and chains that mimic hair and garments and also nod to a past filled with brutality and violence, especially—but not limited to—the transatlantic slave trade.
With their eyes closed, Bey’s figures exude a serene power and dignity in the face of historical injustices, which are woven into the fabric of our present. The show pairs the artist’s work with pieces by Andy Warhol and Jean-Michel Basquiat from the institution’s permanent collection, delving into the way all three explore themes of identity and society.
If you’re in Pittsburgh, you can see Homecoming through October 12. Discover more on Bey’s Instagram.
